title: USDA Food Price Outlook Lifts the 2027 Menu Price Forecast to 3.6 Percent: Budget Food Cost by Location From the Books at the Wholesale Midpoints, Price the High Bound by Category, and Set the Invoice Trigger That Reprices the Menu
excerpt: The November 2026 USDA Food Price Outlook lifts the 2027 restaurant price forecast to 3.6 percent while its wholesale midpoints for beef, pork, and poultry are flat to down, with intervals wide enough to move food cost by five points. Here is how to build the 2027 food cost budget by location from the purchase mix in the books, price the midpoint and the high bound, convert both into a food cost percentage against the menu plan, and set the invoice-based trigger that reprices the menu.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Restaurant group worksheet for the USDA Food Price Outlook November 2026 release, showing three locations' purchase mix by category, the 2027 wholesale midpoint and high-bound cost change, the food cost percentage against a 3.6 percent menu plan, and the invoice price index trigger
content:
The USDA Food Price Outlook published this week puts 2027 restaurant menu prices up 3.6 percent, while its wholesale forecasts for beef, pork, and poultry sit flat to down at the midpoint and swing 20 to 30 points at the bounds. Budget 2027 food cost by location from the books, and set the trigger that reprices the menu.

Why the USDA Food Price Outlook matters now

The Economic Research Service released the November edition of its Food Price Outlook on 2026-11-24. It is the first edition with a full set of 2027 forecasts by category, and the headline numbers moved. Food-away-from-home prices, the index that tracks what restaurants charge, are now forecast to rise 3.6 percent in 2027, with an interval of 1.6 to 5.5 percent. All food is forecast at 3.0 percent, with an interval of -0.7 to 6.9 percent, and food-at-home at 1.9 percent, with an interval of -3.4 to 7.8 percent.

A month earlier the picture was softer. The October edition, as reported by Food World News on 2026-10-26, had 2027 restaurant prices at 2.8 percent, all food at 1.7 percent, and grocery prices at 1.0 percent. In one revision the menu price forecast rose 0.8 points and the all-food forecast 1.3 points. Any 2027 budget built in October on the old midpoints is already stale.

The timing is the reason to act this week rather than in January. Most operators lock 2027 budgets in December, and the November edition is the last one before that. The next edition is scheduled for 2026-12-23, after many budgets are approved. And the margin for error is thin: the National Restaurant Association's 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry release of 2026-02-12 reported that 42 percent of operators said their restaurant was not profitable in 2025, and that more than 9 in 10 cite food among their significant cost challenges.

Coverage of the release reports the headline. Ag Bull Trading, on 2026-11-24, noted the revision from 1.7 to 3.0 percent and that eggs and pork are the only grocery categories expected to get cheaper. Budget guides written before the release, such as the 2027 food cost budget checklist from Basis Point Hospitality, updated 2026-11-02, cite the October edition and recommend base, high, and low cases by commodity group. None of it does three things an operator needs: use the wholesale series rather than the grocery index for purchases, turn the published intervals into a dollar exposure by location from the purchase mix in the books, and define the invoice-based trigger that decides when the menu gets repriced. That is what follows.

Budget purchases at the wholesale series, not the grocery index

The Outlook publishes two families of forecasts. The consumer price series (food-at-home and its categories) measures what shoppers pay at retail. The producer price series measures farm-level and wholesale prices, which sit closer to what a distributor charges a restaurant. A restaurant that budgets beef purchases on the retail beef index of 4.1 percent is budgeting on grocery shelf prices. The wholesale beef forecast for 2027 is 0.7 percent. The two numbers answer different questions.

The table lists the series a kitchen buys against, with the 2026 and 2027 midpoints and the 2027 interval from the ERS data files for producer prices and consumer prices, both updated 2026-11-24. Where ERS publishes no wholesale series, the retail series is the fallback and is marked as such. Eggs are the exception the other way: ERS publishes only a farm-level egg series, forecast at -11.4 percent for 2027 with an interval from -69.3 to 179 percent, which swings far more than delivered shell-egg prices, so the retail egg index is the better budget proxy.

Two things stand out. At the midpoint, 2027 wholesale costs are close to flat: the three proteins that dominate most purchase mixes are forecast at 0.7, -11.5, and -5.3 percent, after a 2026 in which wholesale beef rose 8.9 percent and fats and oils rose 19.8 percent. And the intervals are enormous. Wholesale beef's 2027 range spans 51 points. A budget that carries only the midpoint carries none of that information.

Three locations, one QuickBooks file, one budget: the walk-through

Call it Tidewater Hospitality: a steakhouse, a brunch cafe, and a fast-casual chicken counter in one QuickBooks Online file, with a class per location and food cost split into sub-accounts by category. Annualized 2026 food purchases are $1,200,000, $700,000, and $900,000, and 2026 food cost runs 32.0, 28.0, and 30.0 percent of food sales. The figures are illustrative; the sequence is the point.

Step one: build the purchase mix per location from the books

Run food cost by sub-account and class for the trailing twelve months and express each category as a share of the location's purchases. The steakhouse is 38 percent beef, 12 percent produce, 10 percent seafood, 8 percent dairy, 6 percent poultry, 5 percent pork, 5 percent bakery, 4 percent fats and oils, 4 percent beverages, and 8 percent other. The cafe is 15 percent eggs, 15 percent produce, 14 percent dairy, 14 percent bakery, 12 percent pork, 6 percent poultry, 6 percent beef, 6 percent beverages, 5 percent fats and oils, and 7 percent other. The chicken counter is 35 percent poultry, 14 percent produce, 12 percent bakery, 10 percent fats and oils, 7 percent beverages, 6 percent dairy, 4 percent beef, 4 percent pork, and 8 percent other. If the file books every broadline invoice to one Food Purchases account, the split comes from the distributor's item-level velocity report, mapped once to the categories above and kept as a saved mapping.

Step two: price the midpoint

Multiply each share by the 2027 midpoint in the table and add the products. The steakhouse comes to +0.3 percent, about $3,300 on $1.2 million, because flat beef and a small pork and poultry saving offset dairy, seafood, and fats. The cafe comes to -1.0 percent, about $6,900 saved, driven by pork at -11.5 and eggs at -2.5. The chicken counter comes to -1.3 percent, about $11,600 saved, almost entirely poultry. Across the group the midpoint budget is roughly $15,000 below 2026 purchases at 2026 volumes. That is the number most budgets stop at.

Step three: price the high bound and find where it sits

Now repeat the calculation with the upper interval limit for each category. The steakhouse comes to +20.1 percent, about $241,000, and beef alone is 57 percent of that exposure. The cafe comes to +19.6 percent, about $137,000, with eggs at roughly a quarter of it. The chicken counter comes to +15.5 percent, about $139,500, with poultry at roughly a quarter. The group's high-bound exposure is about $518,000, against a midpoint saving of $15,000. The low bound runs the other way: the steakhouse at its lower limits would see purchases fall about 15 percent, roughly $181,000. The budget should state all three numbers per location, because the decisions that follow depend on which one shows up.

Step four: convert cost into food cost percentage with the menu plan

Food cost percentage for 2027 equals the 2026 percentage times one plus the purchase cost change, divided by one plus the menu price change, holding volume and usage constant. If each location takes the industry's 3.6 percent, the steakhouse goes from 32.0 to 31.0 percent at the midpoint and 37.1 percent at the high bound. The cafe goes from 28.0 to 26.8 percent, or 32.3 percent at the high bound. The chicken counter goes from 30.0 to 28.6 percent, or 33.4 percent. At the midpoint, a 3.6 percent menu increase takes more than a point out of food cost at every location, which is also the argument for taking less than 3.6 where traffic is soft. At the high bound, 3.6 percent recovers less than a third of the cost increase at the steakhouse. The menu plan and the cost plan have to be written together, and tested against the actual split of price, cost, and usage every period once the year starts.

Step five: set the trigger from invoices, not from the news

The published interval tells the operator how far a category can move; it does not tell them when it is moving. For that, build a purchase price index per category per location: the twenty highest-spend items in each category, price per unit from each period's invoices, weighted by 2026 spend, indexed to the December 2026 period at 100. Then write the trigger into the budget. For the steakhouse, a beef index above 108 for two consecutive periods means the four beef entrees are repriced by a stated amount or the feature shifts to a lower-cost cut, decided now and approved now. For the cafe, eggs above 115 means the egg-heavy plates are repriced or portioned. For the counter, poultry above 106 means the combo price moves. Set the reverse trigger as well: pork below 92 at the cafe means the saving is checked against portion spec so it reaches the profit and loss instead of the plate. Re-run the midpoint and high-bound budget when ERS publishes the December edition on 2026-12-23 and each month after; the point of a monthly forecast is that the budget moves with it.

Step six: put the budget where the books can test it

Load the budget as food cost by category, by class, by period, not as one food line per location. Phase it by the 2026 seasonal pattern per period rather than evenly, so a January produce spike doesn't read as a variance. Budget usage, not purchases: usage equals beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory, so a stocking week before a holiday isn't a cost overrun and the period-end count is part of the close. Keep the denominator consistent: food sales net of sales tax, with comps and employee meals handled the same way the 2026 percentage was computed. Vendor rebates and credits are credits to food cost in the period earned, not income. With that structure, the profit and loss by location shows budget against actual by category every period, and a variance can be split into price, usage, and mix instead of argued about. Groups running several entities or files can hold the budget and the comparison in one multi-entity view rather than a spreadsheet per location.

Time: two hours for the mix and the mapping, an hour for the three prices per location, an hour to agree triggers with the chefs, an hour to load the budget. The alternative is a single-line food budget at last year plus 3 percent, which is wrong at the midpoint and silent about the half-million-dollar bound.

Accounting controls for the 2027 food cost budget

Source data: the ERS Food Price Outlook summary and the two data files dated 2026-11-24, with the edition recorded, because the forecasts change monthly; the trailing twelve months of food cost by sub-account and class from the books; the distributor's item-level velocity report where accounts are not split by category; the saved mapping from item or vendor to category and from category to ERS series; period-end inventory counts by location; 2026 food sales by class net of sales tax; and the 2026 food cost percentage by location as computed in the file, not from memory.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Category share equals category purchases divided by location purchases. Midpoint cost change equals the sum of share times the 2027 midpoint; high-bound and low-bound changes use the interval limits the same way. Dollar exposure equals the change times 2026 purchases at 2026 volume. The 2027 food cost percentage equals the 2026 percentage times one plus the cost change, divided by one plus the menu price change. The purchase price index per category equals the spend-weighted price per unit of the tracked items divided by the December 2026 baseline, times 100. Usage equals beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory. Purchases debit food cost; vendor credits and rebates credit food cost; an increase in ending inventory debits the inventory asset and credits food cost, and a decrease does the reverse. Food cost is a flow measure for the period; inventory is a balance at the count date.

Review: a second person, the controller or the outside accountant, confirms that the category shares sum to 100 percent per location and tie to the trailing-twelve-month food cost in the file, that each category is mapped to the ERS series named in the table and the eggs and seafood proxies are flagged, that the interval limits were transcribed from the ERS data files rather than from a news summary, that the menu price assumption per location is the one the operator approved, that the period-end count supporting usage was taken and signed, and that the purchase price index uses the same items and units each period. Any category without a mapping is an open item, not a presumed zero.

Decision: the operator owns the menu price assumption per location and the trigger levels, and signs the responses attached to each trigger before the year starts. The chef at each location owns the portion spec and the substitution list behind the trigger. The controller owns the budget load, the period-end count, and the monthly re-run when a new Outlook edition appears. Nobody budgets food as one line.

Limits and common mistakes

The ERS forecasts are national annual averages. A distributor's contract price, a regional market, and a specific cut or grade will all move differently from the published series, and the Outlook states that ERS does not forecast industry-level producer prices for processed foods. The intervals are the ranges ERS publishes with each forecast; they describe statistical uncertainty, not a prediction of a shock. The Outlook says nothing about labor, the other half of prime cost. Tidewater Hospitality, its three locations, and every figure above are illustrative.

Don't budget purchases on the food-at-home index. It is a grocery price series; the wholesale series are closer to what the kitchen pays.

Don't carry the midpoint alone. The 2027 ranges are wide enough to move food cost by five points at a protein-heavy location, and the budget should say so.

Don't use the farm-level egg series as a delivered-price proxy without saying so. Its interval runs from -69 to +179 percent.

Don't apply one group-wide cost assumption to every location. The mix is what drives the number, and the mix differs by concept.

Don't budget purchases and call it food cost. Without the period-end count, a stocking week looks like a variance and a short count looks like a saving.

Don't let a cost drop disappear. A trigger for a falling index is as useful as one for a rising index, because portion creep absorbs savings quietly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the November 2026 USDA Food Price Outlook forecast for 2027?

The edition released November 24, 2026 forecasts food-away-from-home prices up 3.6 percent in 2027, with an interval of 1.6 to 5.5 percent, all food up 3.0 percent, with an interval of -0.7 to 6.9 percent, and food-at-home up 1.9 percent, with an interval of -3.4 to 7.8 percent. At the wholesale level the 2027 midpoints are beef up 0.7 percent, pork down 11.5 percent, poultry down 5.3 percent, dairy up 2.8 percent, and fats and oils up 3.1 percent.

Should a restaurant budget 2027 food cost on the food-at-home forecast?

No. Food-at-home is the retail grocery index. Restaurants buy at wholesale, and ERS publishes producer price forecasts for wholesale beef, pork, poultry, dairy, fats and oils, and wheat flour, plus farm-level series for eggs, fruits, and vegetables. Budget each purchase category on the series closest to what the distributor charges, and fall back to the retail series only where no wholesale series exists, such as seafood and beverages.

How do I turn the USDA forecast into a food cost budget by location?

Take the trailing twelve months of food purchases by category and location from the books, express each category as a share of that location's purchases, multiply each share by the 2027 midpoint for its ERS series, and add the products. Repeat with the upper and lower interval limits to get the high and low bounds. Multiply each result by 2026 purchases for the dollar exposure, and divide one plus the cost change by one plus the planned menu price change, times the 2026 percentage, to get the 2027 food cost percentage.

What does the 3.6 percent food-away-from-home forecast mean for my menu prices?

It is the forecast average change in restaurant prices nationally, not a recommendation. At the wholesale midpoints, a 3.6 percent menu increase would lower food cost percentage by more than a point at most locations, which argues for taking less where traffic is soft. At the upper bound of the cost interval, 3.6 percent recovers only part of the increase at a protein-heavy location. Set the menu assumption per location alongside the cost budget, and attach a trigger that reprices specific items when the invoice price index crosses a stated level.

Why are the 2027 prediction intervals so wide, and how should a budget handle them?

The 2027 intervals are wide because the forecast horizon is more than a year and the series that drive them, such as cattle, eggs, and vegetables, have moved sharply in recent years. A budget handles that by carrying three numbers per location, midpoint, high bound, and low bound, by tracking an invoice-based purchase price index per category each period, and by re-running the budget when ERS publishes the next edition, which is scheduled for December 23, 2026.

Once each location's budget carries the mix, the three prices, and the trigger, the operator can see in December what the first quarter would otherwise reveal: which location is exposed to beef, which saving will vanish into portions, and when the menu has to move.
